item.title: INSTRUCTION: Tigers and the Taj: How to Combine Them in One Trip
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
The Taj Mahal and a tiger safari are two of India's best early-morning experiences. With some planning, you can include both on one trip. The Taj is closed to general visitors on Fridays, tiger parks close for the monsoon, and the nearest tiger reserve is a half-day drive from Agra. This guide covers timing, routes, and costs for travelers combining the two. Ranthambore's core safari zones normally close from July through September. Other tourism zones may remain open, subject to weather and park restrictions. The core zones of Madhya Pradesh's reserves normally reopen in October, while buffer zones stay open year-round. The Taj is most pleasant from October to March, but dense fog in December and January can hide it completely and delay flights and trains around Delhi and Agra. Allow a spare half-day before any international flight in winter. Tigers are easier to spot from April to June, when animals gather near water, though temperatures can reach 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 C) or higher. February and March offer a good balance of clear weather and dry forest. These months are popular, so book early. Agra sits on the Yamuna, about 124 miles (200 kilometers) south of Delhi. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal for Mumtaz Mahal between about 1632 and 1653, and UNESCO listed it in 1983. It opens 30 minutes before sunrise and closes 30 minutes before sunset. It is closed on Fridays for general viewing. Tour groups tend to arrive between 10 am and 1 pm, so an opening-time visit means softer light, shorter queues, and cooler air. Book tickets online using the official ASI channels. The extra fee for the main mausoleum is the only way to see the inner chamber. Tripods, selfie sticks, food, and large bags are not allowed, and entry is single, with no re-entry. Agra Fort (a UNESCO site, about two hours), Mehtab Bagh for a view of the Taj from across the river, Itimad-ud-Daulah (the "Baby Taj"), and Fatehpur Sikri justify a second morning. Two nights suit most visitors. A hotel near the East or West gate saves time at sunrise. One near Agra Cantt suits train arrivals but adds a longer ride to the monument. Ranthambore, in eastern Rajasthan, is the closest option. A private car from Agra takes roughly 3 hours 20 minutes to 4 hours, making it the safer choice if you want an afternoon safari on your arrival day. Trains run from Agra Fort, Agra Cantt, or Tundla to Sawai Madhopur Junction in about 4 hours 15 minutes to 6 hours, but they can sell out weeks ahead from October to April and may run late. Hotels along Ranthambore Road are 10 to 15 minutes from the station. Madhya Pradesh is a bigger commitment. Bandhavgarh is more than 400 miles (650 km) from Agra, and the fastest train takes about 13.5 hours. Many travelers go by road in stages instead, through Orchha and Khajuraho, then on to Bandhavgarh via Panna. Airports at Khajuraho and Jabalpur offer alternatives, so check current schedules before committing to a long road leg. Ranthambore was a royal hunting ground and became a national park in 1980. A tenth-century fort stands inside it. A 2026 report put Rajasthan's tiger count at 149, with 72 in Ranthambore. The park allots zones by computer, so visitors cannot choose. Zones 1 to 5 are the core, and zones 6 to 10 are buffer areas. Zone 3, around the lakes and ruins, is the most photogenic and the most crowded. Book at least three safaris across at least two zones, since a sighting can never be guaranteed. One travel guide estimates the chance at roughly 70 to 80 percent over four summer safaris and 50 to 60 percent in winter. These figures are unofficial. Six-seat jeeps allow quieter viewing than 20-seat canters. From October to January, morning drives run from about 6:30 to 10:00 am and afternoon drives from about 2:30 to 6:00 pm. Timings change with the season. A good naturalist reads alarm calls from langurs and spotted deer and often turns the vehicle before anything is visible, so ask the operator about the guide. Reports say Ranthambore banned mobile phones on safari from January 30, 2026, and made dashcams mandatory on tourist vehicles. Cameras are allowed, sometimes with registration. Confirm the current rules with the park or your operator before you travel. Madhya Pradesh offers a different landscape. Bandhavgarh is known for tiger density and has a fort within its hills. Kanha has the grassland that inspired Kipling's Jungle Book stories. Pench is quieter. Tiger counts for these parks differ between sources, so treat any figure as approximate. Arrive in Delhi and start with Agra, which is easy and mostly on foot, leaving energy for early safari starts. On the Golden Triangle routes, Ranthambore sits between Agra and Jaipur. On the Madhya Pradesh route, the tiger parks come last after the heritage stops. - Six nights: Delhi 1, Agra 2, Ranthambore 2, Jaipur 1. This is tight but allows three safaris. - Nine nights: Delhi 2, Agra 2, Ranthambore 3, Jaipur 2. The extra night at Ranthambore leaves room for a spare safari, and Jaipur still gets two nights for its palaces. - 11 nights: Delhi 1, Agra 2, Orchha 1, Khajuraho 1, Bandhavgarh 3, Kanha 3. This suits wildlife and heritage lovers, but check flights home from Jabalpur or Nagpur. Do not plan the Taj for a Friday. If your route puts you in Agra that day, use it for the fort, Mehtab Bagh, and the Baby Taj. Don't rely on a single safari; treat every tiger as a bonus. Use only official ticket channels for the Taj. In April 2026, the ASI reportedly warned about a fake site selling invalid tickets, so check the web address carefully and never share a bank OTP. Unlicensed guides near the gates sometimes quote wrong fees, so arrange a licensed guide in advance through your hotel or operator and ignore offers from strangers to skip the queue. Avoid tight connections in winter, since fog affects flights and trains. Government fees are only part of the bill. Hotels, cars and guides add up, so ask for a written quote before paying. Single-use plastic is a problem at both the Taj and in the forest, so carry a refillable bottle. Keep your voice down on safari, stay in the vehicle, and never ask a driver to chase an animal. A video from February 2026 showed more than 40 vehicles around a single tigress, showing what crowding can do. A smaller vehicle, a quieter zone, and a patient guide make for a better sighting. Hire licensed guides and local drivers, buy marble inlay from workshops in which you can see the artisans, and do not feed monkeys at the Taj or the fort. Dress modestly at temples and tombs, and ask before photographing people. Can I do the Taj and a safari in one week? Yes. Delhi, Agra, Ranthambore and Jaipur fit in six to seven nights, with three safaris. Which is better for tigers, Ranthambore or Madhya Pradesh? Ranthambore is easier to reach. Bandhavgarh and Kanha are reported to hold more tigers but need more days. When is the best time for both? Late October to March for comfort, or April to June if tigers matter most and you can handle the heat. Can I use my phone on safari? Check the current rules before you go, and bring a proper camera. BizareXpedition, the company that wrote this guide, plans private itineraries along this route. Checked on October 29, 2026. Fees, rules and timetables change, so confirm with the official pages before traveling. - Taj Mahal fees, hours and Friday closure: UP Tourism Taj Mahal site - Fake ticket website warning, April 2026, and the official ASI booking portals: ETV Bharat - Gatimaan Express timings and Friday off: RailMitra and Railway Gazette - Agra to Ranthambore road and rail times and costs: Rome2Rio - Rajasthan tiger counts, July 28, 2026: ThePrint (PTI) - Ranthambore canter fees, April 1, 2026: ETV Bharat (IANS) - Ranthambore phone ban, January 31, 2026: Free Press Journal - Ranthambore dashcam order, January 7, 2026: ThePrint (PTI) - Safari crowding video, February 2026: Wanderlust - Madhya Pradesh core zone reopening dates: Free Press Journal and Outlook Traveller This story was published in partnership with BizareXpedition™.

item.title: IDEA: Seven travel trends that will define 2027
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Seven travel trends that will define 2027 What do fantasy-inspired escapes, nostalgic holidays and a new kind of boys' trip have in common? They reveal how our changing attitudes to everything from technology to personal relationships are influencing where we go and what we want from our holidays. From seeking deeper connection to embracing otherworldly destinations, here are the seven travel trends to watch in 2027. Next year, travellers will increasingly be seeking out places that feel like another world, whether that's spectacular stargazing spots and ancient ruins or landscapes steeped in myth and folklore. According to Booking.com's 2027 travel predictions, 65% of travellers surveyed expressed interest in paranormal travel experiences, including haunted histories and supernatural encounters; while Pinterest Predicts 2026 noted a surge in searches related to mystical landscapes, with "Scotland Highland aesthetic" up 465% and "ethereal places" up 45%. Travel PR firm Lemongrass suggests that the growing popularity of "romantasy" fiction – which blends romance and fantasy – is helping fuel interest in these otherworldly escapes. But the appeal goes beyond beautiful scenery; it's about escaping the everyday and stepping into another world. "Everywhere we look in our cultural research, we see people seeking awe," says cultural futurist Jasmine Bina, CEO of Concept Bureau. "They want to feel connected to something bigger than themselves, to surrender to something that totally envelops them." Try it: Visit Zermatt, a Swiss Alpine village surrounded by dramatic peaks, considered by fans to be the real-life Velaris, the secret city in Sarah J Maas' A Court of Thorns and Roses series. The traditional boys' golf weekend is getting a makeover, with a new generation of group holidays challenging stereotypes about how men travel. According to Lemongrass' 2027 trends report, men's trips are seeing a growing focus on emotional wellbeing, with retreats designed to encourage connection, self-reflection and more open conversations about masculinity. Citing research from Bupa UK, the report notes that 50% of men have struggled with mental health difficulties, set against a backdrop of changing conversations around loneliness, burnout, work-life balance and financial uncertainty. Group trips can provide an opportunity for these discussions, as explorer Levison Wood notes in the report: "What I have learned is that men often speak most honestly when conversation is not the main purpose. They talk while walking, making camp, sharing food or dealing with a challenge together." "I see this trend growing, especially for men," says Bina. "Therapy and self-reflection have seeped into every part of life. We're at a point in culture right now where the definition and permissions of masculinity are greatly expanding." Try it: Both Sides Retreats offer men the chance to reconnect with their sense of purpose in the UK. In 2027, travellers are looking to recapture the carefree joy of childhood, swapping grown up responsibilities for the simple pleasures of being a kid again. According to Expedia, 57% of travellers surveyed are likely to book an "un-adulting" trip in 2027 – rising to 71% among Gen Z and millennials. Travel companies are responding with experiences designed to appeal to this sense of nostalgia and adventure. Walt Disney World has introduced an adults-only lounge at Epcot and offers late-night theme park events, while Universal Studios Japan has launched an adults-only Halloween Horror Nights overnight experience. Elsewhere, adults-only resorts and cruises promise care-free escapes where the practicalities are taken care of. "We increasingly see people having less shame and embracing the things they truly love," says Bina. "I see it less as shirking responsibilities and more about looking for extreme escape. When you talk to people that go on adult-only trips to theme parks, they'll tell you that those places make them feel safer and more optimistic, like there's order in the world again." Try it: Ride the waterslides at Jamaica's Princess Senses The Mangrove Resort, an adults-only all-inclusive resort with water-park access where you don't need to think about anything beyond having fun. As AI becomes part of everyday life, travellers are increasingly seeking something technology can't provide: human connection. While 40% of Americans now use AI for tasks such as travel planning, industry research suggests that shared experiences and meaningful interactions are becoming more important. According to Hilton's 2027 Trends Report, 60% of travellers surveyed are more drawn to water-based wellness activities when they can share them with others. Meanwhile, Skyscanner has seen a rise in large-group bookings. Human connection is worth paying for, says Priceline: in their recent survey, 66% of Americans said they would pay extra for exceptional personal attention. "Everything has become synthetic," says Bina. "Deepfake AI, bosses sending ChatGPT nonsense to their teams, misleading packaging – we are surrounded by the uncanny and the unreal. Connection is scarce, and in high demand." For a growing number of travellers, holidays aren't just about switching off; they're about discovering new interests and switching on your brain. While learning holidays are nothing new, the latest trend puts a greater emphasis on hobbies and the pleasure of play. According to Hilton, Gen Z travellers are nearly twice as likely as baby boomers to want to return home with a new interest they can continue pursuing, while holiday rental platform Vrbo has seen rising demand for "hobby hubs" – properties suited to everything from crafting retreats and photography weekends to antique hunting jaunts. "This is a really beautiful incarnation of our overall cultural shift toward play," says Bina. "Hobbies get us into our bodies and into flow states in a way that modern, commercialised wellness perhaps never could." Try it: Learn Spanish while walking the Camino de Santiago with Responsible Travel, combining mornings language lessons with afternoon hikes through northern Spain. The minibreak is getting even shorter. In 2027, travellers are increasingly embracing one-night getaways, whether it's to attend a concert or sporting event, celebrate a milestone or simply enjoy a quick escape. According to Hotels.com, 79% of travellers surveyed plan to book a one-night stay in the coming year, rising to 83% among Gen Z and millennials. Searches for one-night getaways have also increased by nearly 10% year on year. Dubbed "trip snacking", these bite-sized breaks offer a quick reset between holidays, with 71% of respondents saying they help tide them over until their next trip. Against a backdrop of rising living costs and economic uncertainty, the appeal of a shorter, potentially more affordable escape is easy to understand. "Short trips are part of a broader trend toward minification, like little treat culture, tiny homes and microweddings," says Bina. "It's economically driven but also well suited for peoples' increasingly busy lives. Smaller doesn't mean less – it actually means the opposite. When something is truncated, we need it to be that much more intense in order to satisfy our desires." Try it: Book a microbreak through Staycation, a platform offering hotels for 24 hours, 48 hours or even just a few hours across Europe. In 2027, the ultimate status symbol may be an experience that nobody else can replicate. From one-off cultural events to rare encounters with people and places, travellers are seeking one-of-a-kind experiences. FINN Partners calls this "unrepeatable travel", experiences whose value lie in their rarity and authenticity rather than their price tag. Bina says that this is all about how the idea of status is changing. "Columbia University professor Silvia Bellezza says we gain status in culture by creating distance from the norm, and for a long time, money was that distance," says Bina. "If you had enough money to travel to revered hotspots, your wealth equalled distance. But now that anybody can fake wealth on social media, money doesn't provide distance anymore. So the new status comes from unrepeatable experiences, a way of creating distance by the way of access and knowledge that nobody else has." Try it: Cruise the Nile during the total solar eclipse on 2 August 2027, when Luxor will be in the path of totality. Specialist voyages will bring travellers together with scientists and astronomers to witness the rare celestial event. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Diving the Sea of Cortez: What a Liveaboard Trip Really Looks Like
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Few places pack as much marine life into one stretch of water as the Sea of Cortez, the long arm of the Pacific between mainland Mexico and the Baja California peninsula. Day trips from shore reach only part of it. Remote seamounts, sea lion colonies, and protected reefs are often hours away by boat, so many divers choose a liveaboard. If you are thinking about booking one of the Nautilus Liveaboards diving trips in the Sea of Cortez, it helps to know what life on board is like, from the first briefing to the last night dive. Why the Sea of Cortez Is Worth a Liveaboard Jacques Cousteau famously called the Sea of Cortez "the world's aquarium," and the name still fits. Deep, nutrient-rich water rises along the Gulf's underwater ridges and feeds plankton, which then draws in everything from tiny reef fish to large pelagic species. A single week can include playful California sea lions, schooling jacks, mobula and eagle rays, moray eels, and nudibranchs. With some luck, you may also see hammerhead sharks, giant mantas, or whale sharks, depending on the season. Many of the best sites lie far from the main towns of La Paz and Cabo San Lucas. A liveaboard solves this: the boat moves while you eat and sleep, so every day starts at a new site instead of a long morning commute across open water. The rhythm of a liveaboard is simple, and most divers find it relaxing after a day or two. Days usually start early with coffee and a light snack before the first dive. The crew briefs you on the site layout, currents, depth limits, and animals you are likely to meet. Early dives often have the calmest surface conditions and the most active marine life, especially at seamounts where pelagic species gather. After a full breakfast and a surface interval, you do the second dive. Lunch follows, then time to rest, review photos, or watch the coastline from the sun deck. Surface intervals are part of the experience. Dolphins and even whales are sometimes seen from the boat between dives. An afternoon dive is often followed by a night dive, when the reef changes character. Octopuses hunt openly, crustaceans come out of hiding, and you may see bioluminescence. Nautilus advertises up to four dives daily, including night dives, depending on the itinerary and conditions. Divers ultimately choose how many they want to participate in. Every route is different, but a few experiences define diving in this region. - Sea lion encounters: At colonies such as Los Islotes* near Isla Espíritu Santo, young sea lions often swim right up to divers, twisting and blowing bubbles. For many people, it is the highlight of the trip. - Seamount diving: Offshore pinnacles like El Bajo are known for strong currents and big-animal sightings, including schooling hammerheads in season. - Wrecks: Several sunken vessels near La Paz have become artificial reefs covered in life, rewarding photographers. - Protected reefs: Marine parks such as Cabo Pulmo show what decades of protection can do, with dense fish populations and healthy hard coral. *Los Islotes closes to diving and snorkeling during the summer breeding season and typically reopens Sept. 1. Summer itineraries may visit other sea lion colonies instead. The main liveaboard season runs from summer into autumn, roughly July to November. Water temperatures in late summer can reach 29-30°C (mid-80s°F), and visibility is often 20-30 meters. Later in the season, the water cools, and visibility can drop, so check conditions for your dates. A 3mm wetsuit is usually enough at the warmest time of year. Bring a thicker suit or hood if you get cold easily or plan several dives a day. A surface marker buoy, reef-safe sunscreen, motion-sickness remedies, and a light jacket for windy evenings on deck are also worth packing. You don't need to be an expert to enjoy this kind of trip. Open Water certification and good buoyancy control are usually enough, since guides lead the dives and some sites, particularly inside national parks, require a guide anyway. More advanced divers will enjoy the current-swept seamounts and the chance to log many dives in a short time. Everyone gets the same advantages: little travel time, plenty of time in the water and a front-row seat to one of the richest marine ecosystems on the planet. A liveaboard in the Sea of Cortez is less about luxury than about immersion. You wake up next to remote islands, dive several times a day, share stories over dinner, and fall asleep while the boat heads to the next site. For divers who want to see the Gulf at its wildest, it is one of the most efficient and memorable ways to explore it. This story was published in partnership with Nautilus Adventures.

item.title: A new Eurostar route from London is about to launch to this beloved European city, just in time for Christmas
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
With December fast approaching, it's time to start planning those festive getaways. But where should you go for a long weekend in Europe? And is it time to discover somewhere new, away from the usual tourist hotspots? If you're looking for inspiration, Eurostar might have just the answer. From December, a new direct route will make it easier than ever to reach one of Belgium's most exciting cities, just in time for Christmas. Eurostar announced earlier this year that travellers will be able to book and travel on direct journeys from London St Pancras to Belgium’s second-biggest city, Antwerp-Centraal, from 14 December. With just a month to go until the launch, tickets are already on sale, with one-way fares starting from £51. When the new route was first announced in July, Eurostar said: “Adding Antwerp as a direct stop on our London-Amsterdam services will make journeys to the city quicker and more convenient, providing customers with a more comfortable city centre to city centre travel experience.” At the moment, getting from London to Antwerp by train can take around three hours and 15 minutes and involves getting the Eurostar to Brussels then changing onto a separate Belgian train for the rest of the journey to Antwerp. The new direct route cuts travel time by around 30 minutes, bringing the journey to around two hours and 45 minutes. Over the past year, there’s been lots of discussion on whether Eurostar would be introducing new direct connections to European destinations like Switzerland, Cologne and Frankfurt. The rail firm has pledged to launch these proposed new routes in the early 2030s, but Eurostar will bring in this new direct route to Antwerp on 14 December – just in time to discover the city in all its festive glory. The trains, which currently run between London and Amsterdam, will introduce the direct connection to Antwerp with existing stops at Lille-Europe, Brussels-Midi, Rotterdam-Centraal and Amsterdam-Centraal. However, there is a slight catch to this new direct route. You can only travel to Antwerp directly from London on the outward leg of the journey, and it doesn’t cover the return part of the trip. Eurostar said this is due to customs and border issues and that a return direct route through to London would require dedicated UK border and customs facilities at Antwerp-Centraal, which it has no current plans for. Travellers returning to London will instead need to take a Belgian SNCB train to Brussels-Midi, where they can complete UK border and security checks before boarding the Eurostar to London. According to the timetable published earlier this year, direct trains are scheduled to depart London St Pancras as early as 6.16am, with morning and evening departures also available. Those planning a return trip should allow a little longer for the journey home, which Eurostar estimates at around three hours and 50 minutes, including the change at Brussels-Midi. Tickets for both legs of the return journey can be booked together on Eurostar's website. Antwerp is a particularly gorgeous destination in December, when the city's annual Christmas market takes over the historic centre. Running from 4 December 2026 to 3 January 2027, the festivities include market stalls, an ice rink and plenty of opportunities for Christmas shopping. Beyond the festive celebrations, Antwerp offers an array of great restaurants and bars, fabulous independent boutiques and some impressive art galleries to explore.

item.title: JetBlue is Launching a New Domestic First Class—and We Got a First Look
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Flying domestic with JetBlue just got an upgrade. On Wednesday, November 11, the airline introduced BlueFirst, a brand-new domestic first class product, ahead of its debut flight on December 8. The cabin is a dedicated section in the first three rows, arranged two-by-two (read: no middle seats). It will be installed across the airline's fleet on planes that do not already have a Mint business class cabin, bringing a domestic first class to the shorter routes for which JetBlue is more commonly known. As Stephanie Evans Greene, the airline’s senior vice president of marketing and brand, tells Condé Nast Traveler, the idea is "premium, but not pretentious." BlueFirst will begin rolling out across JetBlue’s fleet in early December, beginning with the carrier’s daily Boston–Fort Lauderdale flight and soon followed by its popular Fort Lauderdale–New York LaGuardia route. The new cabin is a big shift for JetBlue, an airline that for most of its 26 years in business flew economy seats only. The one exception is Mint, a lie-flat business class available on the airline's transcontinental and transatlantic routes, like New York to Los Angeles and London. To be clear: BlueFirst is not a version of Mint, and the two will never appear on the same plane. Mint planes keep Mint, and BlueFirst goes on every other aircraft. Where Mint is a bed, BlueFirst is a recliner, built for the shorter leisure routes that make up most of JetBlue's network. To test out the BlueFirst product, we checked out the first aircraft with the new cabins installed on the ground at New York—JFK. Here's everything travelers should know before booking. What are the new BlueFirst seats like? As for the seat itself, the first thing that will stand out to travelers is just how much more space there is. BlueFirst has only three rows—12 seats total—and each seat is about three inches wider than a standard economy seat, with room to spare in every direction. The seat is spacious enough to hold a passenger and a laptop bag next to them (or a large purse, in my case), and the space in front is just as generous, with up to seven extra inches of legroom compared with JetBlue's regular Main seats. It reclines five inches too, though the recline takes a bit of pressure (hold the button and push back on the seat firmly). Press the button again, and the seat pops right back up. In true JetBlue fashion—this is, after all, the airline that built its name on being the un-stuffy one—there's no curtain cutting the BlueFirst cabin off from the rest of the plane. The seat cushion is made with Tuft & Needle's T&N Flex foam (yes, the mattress company), developed just for JetBlue. It's squishy enough to comfortably sink into, and it responds as you shift, in both the bottom cushion and the backrest. The adjustable headrest also has wings that fold in to cradle your head. "I'll go on record and say I think they're some of the most comfortable recline seats that are out there in domestic first class," Greene says. What other perks come with BlueFirst? Aside from the bigger, more comfortable seat, BlueFirst gives travelers a slew of other perks. At every seat, there's a 13.3-inch screen with Bluetooth for personal earbuds, USB-A, USB-C, and a regular outlet, plus JetBlue's free Wi-Fi. The overhead bins above the cabin are reserved for BlueFirst passengers, so boarding doesn't come with the usual scramble for space, and each large bifold tray table has a stand for your phone or tablet. Travelers also get a blanket and an amenity kit with socks, earbuds, mouthwash, and OSEA Malibu skincare products, including a lip balm, hand cream, and the fan-favorite calming pulse point oil. What's more, the perks start before passengers even get on the plane: BlueFirst comes with priority check-in, a faster security lane at more than 30 airports, and Group 1 boarding. Most BlueFirst fares come with two free checked bags—even BlueFirst Base, the cheapest of the three, includes one checked bag. What food and drinks are served in BlueFirst? The dining options in BlueFirst depend on how long your flight is. A bento-inspired box is served on flights of 899 miles or more, with an entrée, a side, and a dessert. The exact menu changes based on the route. Dinner might be a tortellini pasta salad with marinated green olives, a pastrami sandwich with a citrusy cabbage salad, or sesame noodles with crispy wontons and a Szechuan dip. The desserts are a highlight: the pasta comes with a carrot cake with a caramel icing top that's deliciously moist (my personal favorite), and there are colorful macarons and a pistachio chocolate cake on other menus. Breakfast runs from hazelnut-ricotta crêpes to a sweet potato and bean bowl with guacamole and hot sauce, a poached pear, and blueberry chia pudding. There are also kosher, vegan, and gluten-free versions of the boxes. The whole meal arrives at once in the box, and because there's no oven on board, everything is served cold or at room temperature—something JetBlue regulars have been quick to point out. However, BlueFirst travelers can also indulge in a basket of premium snacks that includes Swedish candy from Sockerbit, Tosi snack bars, Wholesome Bakery cookies, and Cape Cod chips. Drinks in this section of the cabin deserve their own mention, because BlueFirst's come with a twist you won't find on other US airlines. Everything is ordered right from the seatback screen in Mixologist Mode, which lets you build your own cocktail (or mocktail) instead of choosing from a list. You start with a base—a spirit, a soft drink, coffee, a mixer—and add up to four items in total from the full drink menu. The crew then brings the ingredients right to your separate pop-out cocktail tray, and you mix it yourself. There's a limit of two drinks per order, but once the first round lands, you can start the next. The drinks come in real glassware from Fable, on handmade watercolor coasters by New York-based illustrator Danielle Rose Fisher. For anyone not playing bartender, there's also wine from Parcelle, coffee from Cometeer and Joe Coffee, and Smith Teamaker teas. BlueFirst tickets are currently on sale for travel dates beginning in December. The cabins will be added to more than 30 routes throughout 2026; you'll start seeing the new seats on flights from JFK to Cancún, Liberia, and San Juan beginning in January. However, even on those inaugural routes, not every flight will have BlueFirst right away (it depends on whether a fitted plane is operating that flight). Just over a dozen planes will have the cabin by the end of this year, with the rest of the fleet following through 2027. By the end of next year, the retrofit should be nearly done, covering every JetBlue plane that doesn't have Mint. Until then, it's worth double-checking before booking since JetBlue notes BlueFirst may only be available on select flights or dates, and planes can be swapped at a moment’s notice depending on equipment needs and maintenance.

item.title: These epic new Nile cruises put Egypt's ancient wonders within reach
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Call it the ultimate Nile River cruise experience. River cruise giant Viking has unveiled an epic new itinerary that sails the entire 600-mile stretch of the waterway between Cairo in the north and Aswan in the south. Dubbed the Grand Nile Journey, Viking's 19-day trip revives a longer Nile cruise route that dates back to the late 1800s, when paddle steamers carried travelers from Cairo on the 465-mile journey south to Luxor, home to some of ancient Egypt's most famous temples and burial grounds. From there, the vessels would continue to Aswan, another 130 miles to the south, with stops at ancient temples along the way. Nowadays, most Nile River sailings skip the first 465 miles of this historic route, with ships only traveling along the 130-mile stretch of the Nile between Luxor and Aswan. Passengers reach the ships by flying from Cairo to Luxor, typically after a few days exploring Cairo. Only a handful of vessels currently operate a longer itinerary of the sort that Viking has announced — and none at the luxury level for which Viking is known on the river. Kicking off in 2028 but available to book now, Viking's new Grand Nile Journeys will begin with a three-night stay at a luxury hotel in Cairo (the line often puts guests in the elegant Fairmont Nile City, along the banks of the river). Then, passengers board the line's one-of-a-kind, all-suite vessel Viking Ra for the 14-night journey south to Aswan. The voyages will include stops at ancient sites along the 450-mile stretch from Cairo to Luxor that most Nile River travelers never see, including the 4,600-year-old Meidum Pyramid near Beni Suef and the striking cliffside Noble Tombs of Beni Hasan. Other rare stops will include a visit to Tell el-Amarna, the once-lost royal desert capital founded by the Pharaoh Akhenaten, and the Abydos Temple, famous for drawings of ancient pilgrims to the sacred Festival of Osiris. After a week traveling south along this lesser-visited stretch of the Nile, the Viking Ra will arrive in Luxor for another week of travel southward along the more popular parts of the river. An extended stop in Luxor will bring visits to the temples of Luxor and Karnak, the royal tombs of the Valley of the Kings and the Temple of Seti I at Abydos. Additional stops include the Temple of Horus in Edfu and the Temple of Philae near Aswan, among other sites in this area. By following this long route from Cairo to Aswan, the new Grand Nile Journeys will echo the long Nile sailing that Agatha Christie made famous in her 1937 novel "Death on the Nile." She wrote the book after taking one of the long journeys in 1933 on the Thomas Cook & Son luxury paddle steamer S.S. Sudan. The first few days of each of the new Grand Nile Journeys in Cairo will include visits to the Great Pyramids of Giza, the Great Sphinx and the Grand Egyptian Museum. At the end of the trip, passengers will also spend a final night at a hotel in Cairo before departing. Passengers can extend their trips with optional pre- and postcruise land tours that include an extra two-night stay in Cairo and a four-night, fully guided excursion to nearby Jordan for visits to the Dead Sea, Petra and Amman. While dating back to the late 1800s, when Thomas Cook & Son introduced "rapid steamers" that sailed the Nile from Cairo to Aswan, such longer Nile itineraries continued to be common until 1994, when the Egyptian government officially closed the 465-mile stretch of the river between Cairo and Luxor to overnight passenger ships due to security worries. Low water levels and shifting sandbars in the river also played a role. After nearly 20 years of closure, the Egyptian government reopened the Cairo-to-Luxor stretch of the river to cruise vessels in 2012, following extensive river dredging, irrigation upgrades and major security overhauls. But long sailings from Cairo to Aswan have been slow to rebound. Among the handful of other companies offering such trips is Movenpick Hotels & Resorts, which markets 14-night sailings from Cairo to Aswan on the 52-cabin MS Darakum. Planning a cruise? item.title: Korean Air will give New Yorkers a new nonstop option to Seoul
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Korean Air is adding a second New York-area gateway. The SkyTeam Alliance carrier will land at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) with flights from Seoul’s Incheon Airport (ICN) in May 2027, Korean Air said on Thursday. The new route to east of the Hudson River complements its long-standing twice-daily service to New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). Korean Air will offer daily flights to EWR from May 22. It will fly a Boeing 777-300ER on the route. The airline did not say what 777 configuration it will fly to EWR. It flies planes with several layouts, including an older configuration with eight first class suites. United Airlines launched its first-ever nonstop from EWR to ICN in September. The Star Alliance carrier flies a Boeing 787-9 on the route. Korean Air’s new EWR flight comes at a time of change for the airline as it wraps up a merger with fellow Korean carrier Asiana. Korean will complete the customer-facing integration of Asiana on Dec. 17, a combination that will significantly increase its market share at ICN. While the merger does not add any new U.S. destinations to Korean Air’s map, it does increase its presence at JFK to up to four daily flights including Asiana, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows. Future schedules show Korean Air continuing to serve JFK with four daily flights through June 2027. The new EWR flight will complement Korean Air’s JFK services and create a new connection with joint venture partner Delta Air Lines. The carriers have expanded their transpacific options in recent years with new routes, including Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) to ICN on Delta. The partnership allows Delta and Korean Air to coordinate commercial matters, including fares and schedules, between the U.S. and South Korea. Korean Air highlighted the expanded flight options and New Jersey’s pharmaceutical, biotechnology, financial, and logistics industrial clusters for its new EWR route. EWR is Korean Air’s first new U.S. destinations since it added Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) in 2019.

item.title: Design underway on United’s eagerly-awaited Denver Polaris Lounge
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Business-class fliers on United Airlines will soon be able to relax in a fancy new Polaris Lounge at Denver International Airport (DEN). Design work is underway on the new, exclusive lounge at DEN, Aaron McMillan, the managing director of hospitality programs at United, told TPG on Monday. “We’re going to build a mezzanine on top of [the existing] mezzanine and expand the floor plate a little bit,” he said referring to a location at DEN near the end of Concourse A between gates A18 and A20. “We’ll have a two-story Polaris lounge there.” United aims to open the new DEN Polaris Lounge by late 2028 or early 2029, added McMillan. The news comes amid a club building spree by the airline. United opened a massive Washington, D.C.-inspired United Club in the new E Concourse at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) on Tuesday. The space is second in size only to the new club at Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) that opened in October. United is also building a new club at San Francisco International Airport (SFO) that is scheduled to open by the end of the year, and is in talks for new clubs at Southwest Florida International Airport (RSW) in Fort Myers and Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC). The Polaris Lounge is United’s premium airport space accessible only to fliers booked in same-day, long-haul business class or in business or first class on several partner airlines, including All Nippon Airways (ANA) and Lufthansa. The spaces compete with American Airlines’ Flagship Lounges and Delta Air Lines’ Delta One Lounges. United has six Polaris Lounges: Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), IAH, Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), SFO and IAD. DEN is United’s only mainland U.S. hub without a Polaris Lounge. When United opened its first Polaris space at ORD in 2016, lounges were only planned at its main international gateways and not DEN. The Colorado hub boasted only one long-haul nonstop at the time: Tokyo’s Narita Airport (NRT), schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows. Today, United flies five intercontinental routes from DEN: Frankfurt Airport (FRA), London’s Heathrow Airport (LHR), Munich Airport (MUC), Rome Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO) and NRT. It will add its sixth route, to Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), next summer. “Aside from the local departures we’ve grown out of Denver, there’s also a fairly significant number of local customers that are connecting over like Chicago, and Houston, and San Francisco that are traveling Polaris that can take advantage of the product,” said McMillan. And while McMillan was mum on the look and feel of the new Polaris Lounge at DEN, he was confident in one thing: it will not have an outdoor patio. All travelers at DEN have access to the public outdoor patios at the ends of concourses A, B and C. Related reading:

item.title: Georgia’s Entire 78-Mile Appalachian Trail Section Will Require Bear Canisters in 2027
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Hikers on Georgia’s stretch of the Appalachian Trail will need to store their food in a hard-sided canister next year according to a new order from the U.S. Forest Service, a change that follows years of rising bear encounters on the southern miles of the AT. In a press release, the USFS said that the rule would take effect January 1, and would apply to anyone camping in a 1-mile-wide corridor along the entire 78-mile section of the AT, including hikers staying in shelters. The requirement is year-round and also applies to the AT Approach Trail. Alternative food-storage methods like bear hangs and Ursacks will not be allowed. Hikers who violate the order could face a fine of up to $5,000 or 6 months in jail. “With the Appalachian Trail going through the heart of North Georgia’s black bear habitat, we want the hikers who flock here to understand how incredibly valuable these public lands are—for people and for wildlife,” Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest Supervisor Judy Toppins said. “Finding a balance that protects hikers, wildlife, and forest health is our goal.” As visitation to the Appalachian Trail has risen in recent years, human-bear conflicts have too, with a 2025 survey by the Appalachian Trail Conservancy finding that bear reports had risen by 75 percent that year alone. A disproportionate amount of those run-ins happen in Georgia: Morgan Sommerville, the ATC’s director of visitor use management, said that while just 3.5 percent of the AT lies in Georgia, the state accounted for more than 12 percent of its bear encounters. The new requirements represent the largest expansion of food storage rules on the trail yet. Previously, only a few short segments required a canister, such as the 5-mile segment between Jarrard and Neel Gaps in Georgia’s Blood Mountain Wilderness. Hikers who didn’t want to tote a hard-sided container could simply avoid camping in many of those. “The ATC has recommended that overnight campers on the Trail carry a bear-resistant food storage container since 2017 because of how adept bears have become at defeating traditional food hangs and other storage methods,” Somerville said. “This new order along the AT in Georgia will require all overnight hikers and backpackers to use reliable food storage gear—a hard-sided bear canister—on their AT adventures, which will protect themselves and the bears that call the AT home.” Getting AT thru- and section-hikers to embrace the new guidelines could be a challenge. While the ATC has recommended for almost 10 years that hikers carry bear canisters, data suggests that few do. A 2025 survey by The Trek found that 13.6 percent used a canister, compared to 43 percent who used a bear hang and 32.3 percent who chose the riskiest option and slept with their food.

item.title: IDEA: Samaná in Phases: How We Explored the Dominican Republic's Wild Peninsula Together
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Melody is Dominican, so people assume the Dominican Republic holds no surprises for her. Samaná proved otherwise. We loved discovering it together slowly, and that is why we keep pointing independent travelers toward it. Most visitors meet the DR through the resort strip. Samaná is the opposite: a jungle-backed peninsula on the northeast coast where the beaches are still wild, the roads are still slow, and the best plan is often no plan at all. If we could give one piece of advice, it is this: see Samaná in parts, in phases, not all at once. That is how we did it and would do it again. We split the peninsula into two phases: Las Galeras first and Las Terrenas second, with a few unhurried days in each. We let each place have its own rhythm instead of racing between them. Samaná is one of several destinations featured in our Dominican Republic travel guide, which includes more photos and ideas for exploring the country. Driving is difficult in the DR, so we do not assume we will drive everywhere ourselves. We arrange local transport or join a tour, and we build in empty time because island pace is part of the charm here, not a problem to solve. Las Galeras is the sleepy town at the tip of the peninsula, and we chose it as our first phase for a reason. Everything here is close, quiet, and unhurried. The town itself is small and easy, the kind of place where the two of us walk everywhere and the day sorts itself out. The beach that makes Las Galeras worth the trip on its own is Playa Rincón. Go early. In the morning, the sand is empty, the light is soft, and you get the long stretch of beach almost to yourselves before the day fills in. Our favorite rhythm here was a long morning on the sand, a swim, a walk along it, and then a grilled fish lunch at a simple beach spot before the afternoon heat settles in. That easy pattern, an early beach morning and a lazy lunch, is the whole point of giving this phase its own days. The Wild Coves: Playa Frontón and Playa Madama From Las Galeras, the peninsula's wildest beaches are the ones you cannot drive to. You reach Playa Frontón and Playa Madama by boat, or a short hike, and that effort is what keeps them quiet. These are wilder, rockier, and far less visited than the main beaches. The reward is a beach that feels like it belongs to the two of you for the morning. Two things matter here. First, water shoes. They are essential, not optional, because the shoreline is rocky in places and you will want them for getting in and out of the water and for walking the cove edges. Second, cash. Boat rides and simple beach lunches require cash, so carry enough for the day before you set out and don't rely on a fixed timetable. Ask around in Las Galeras for a boat, bring water, and let the morning shape itself. El Limón is the inland break in a beach-heavy trip and is worth a full morning. The walk goes through tropical forest, and the reward is a swim in the natural pool at the base of the waterfall. It is a simple pleasure: forest shade, cool water, and a swim that feels earned after the walk. Go with a local guide. The path is a forest walk, not a marked promenade, and a local guide makes the outing smoother and more enjoyable. Wear shoes you can walk in that can get wet, and leave the rest of the day open so you are not rushing back to the beach. After the quiet of Las Galeras, Las Terrenas was our second phase with a different energy. It is a laid-back, slightly bohemian beach town where the two of you settle in rather than pass through. Days here are slower in a different way: mornings on the beach, long lunches, and evenings built around eating well. The food scene is one of the reasons we love Las Terrenas. It has a French-Caribbean character you don't find everywhere in the DR, and spending a few days here means eating well without trying hard. We keep our evenings simple: a good meal, a walk together, and an early night so the next beach morning starts well. The beaches around Las Terrenas are golden and easy to reach. Playa Bonita and Playa Cosón are the two we return to. The best way to enjoy them is without a plan: walk between them, stop for coffee when you feel like it, and swim when you feel like it. Cosón at sunset is the moment to plan your day around. The whole beach turns gold, the light softens, and it is the kind of evening that makes you glad you did not rush anywhere all day. Go early to find your spot, stay through the sunset, and walk back slowly together. The Other Side of the Peninsula: Mangroves and Los Haitises The bay side of the peninsula is a different world from the ocean beaches and worth a half-day rather than a rushed add-on. Floating through the glassy mangrove channels is quiet, green, and strange in the best way: still water, tangled roots, and birdsong instead of waves. It pairs naturally with a boat trip to Los Haitises, where the caves and bird-filled islets are the main event. Together they show you a side of Samaná that has nothing to do with beaches, and the contrast is what makes the peninsula feel so complete. If your trip falls between January and March, Samaná Bay is one of the world's best places to see humpback whales and is worth reshuffling the whole plan for. This is the one exception to the slow plan: when the whales are in the bay, go. A whale morning is the kind of experience that rearranges everything else around it, and we would not trade it for a beach day. Practical Notes for Doing It Independently Pack water shoes because some of the best coves are rocky. Bring cash for boat rides and beach lunches. Don't try to drive everywhere yourself; arrange transport locally or join a tour. See Samaná in phases, Las Galeras first and Las Terrenas second, and give each phase a few days. Accept that things move at island pace, which is exactly the point. Samaná is the DR at its wildest, and discovering it together, even with one of us being local, is what made it special for us. Slow down on purpose, take it in phases, walk the beaches early, take the boats when they come, and leave room in the plan for the place that surprises you. That is the whole route, and it has never let us down.

item.title: The Historic SS United States Was Sunk off Florida to Become the World’s Largest Artificial Reef
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
As it turns out, it takes a lot to sink a 990-foot ocean liner. The SS United States was supposed to start going down at 1 p.m. Central Time on Wednesday, November 11. Last-minute preparations pushed that to nearly 5 p.m. By 4:45, every valve was open, and the Gulf was pouring in. Then came four more hours of watching a ship refuse to leave. She finally slipped under at 8:59 P.M., twenty-two nautical miles southwest of Destin, Florida, in the Gulf of Mexico, tilting hard to her port side. From a nearby boat, I watched the fastest ocean liner ever built make the slowest exit imaginable. On her maiden voyage in 1952, she beat the Queen Mary’s record by about ten hours. On Veterans Day, the iconic ocean liner needed about four hours just to go under. With this scuttling—a deliberate, controlled sinking—the SS United States becomes the world’s largest artificial reef, surpassing the USS Oriskany, which had held the title since its 2006 sinking. It’s a second life that’s part habitat project and part tourism bet, and it follows years of failed rescue plans and a last-minute court fight. Here’s how a ship once meant to become a museum ended up on the Gulf floor, what it means for the sea around her, and what divers can expect when they finally get to explore her underwater. Why sink her off the Florida Panhandle? Habitat and tourism. The seafloor off Destin and Fort Walton Beach is mostly sand and shell, and natural reef is scarce. Okaloosa County’s tourism department laid out a five-year, $12 million plan to make Destin-Fort Walton Beach the dive capital of Florida, with part of the money coming from tourist-development tax revenue. Visit Pensacola and the Coastal Conservation Association’s Florida chapter signed on as partners. Part of that money funds a multiyear marketing campaign to promote the ship as a diving destination. The SS United States is also slated to join the Florida Panhandle Shipwreck Trail. The state created the trail in 2012 to stimulate tourism, after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. It began with twelve wrecks off Pensacola, Destin, Panama City, and Port St. Joe and has since grown to more than 20. Divers collect passport stickers at each one. These 20 ships are among 48 large vessels sunk by the county since the 1970s. The SS United States now rests in about 180 feet of water. If she landed upright, as early sonar scanning indicates, her upper decks are roughly 50 to 60 feet down. The county says divers of all skill levels can reach the upper decks. While there were once dreams of converting the 990-foot icon into a hotel or museum, she deteriorated to the point that the options came down to the scrapyard or an artificial reef. The liner was abruptly withdrawn from service in 1969. She later spent nearly thirty years docked in Philadelphia, where no one managed to repurpose her. For decades, owners kept hunting for the ship’s second act. In 2016, Crystal Cruises studied a return to sea and called the obstacles insurmountable. By the time a rent fight got the historic ship ordered off a Philadelphia pier in 2024, the nonprofit that owned the vessel says it was left with two options: scrap or “reef her”. Preservationists argue a museum ship was still possible. The conservancy ultimately sold the liner to Okaloosa County, Florida, for $1 million. The county has spent a total of more than $13 million getting it ready to scuttle—remediation, towing, insurance, deployment—and contributing toward the yet-to-be-constructed museum dedicated to the ocean liner. The county’s tourism director calls the project an economic development opportunity and an environmental asset. Its tourism director told NPR the county expects to make back its investment in a couple of years. A last-minute lawsuit nearly stopped the sinking. The SS United States Preservation Foundation sued the Army Corps of Engineers in federal court in Pensacola on November 3, arguing the agency failed to adequately weigh the ship’s toxic coatings under federal environmental law. Three days later, a judge denied the emergency request to halt the sinking, citing the lack of an affidavit and the cost of an injunction. An earlier suit from a separate New York group had already been dismissed in 2025. On the whole, scuttling (or initially sinking) a properly cleaned vessel can house a new ecosystem for fish and other oceanic life. Crews drained and cleaned the fuel tanks of the SS United States, and no explosives were used. The county says it removed 99 percent of the PCB-containing materials, though nobody outside the project has independently verified that number. The open question is the old zinc-chromate primer, which contains hexavalent chromium. Those who still wanted the ship preserved topside say it will leach. The county says it converts underwater into a less toxic form. A Drexel oceanographer called the risk “a little overblown,” while saying he’d still prefer mitigation. The Oriskany, another purpose-sunk vessel off the coast of Destin, which held the title of world’s largest artificial reef until Wednesday is a cautionary precedent. It became a thriving reef, but monitoring also found elevated PCBs in some of its fish. Algae, barnacles, and sponges settle on the steel first. Corals can follow, then small fish, then the predators that hunt them. Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution is tracking the process at about 132 tagged spots on the wreck, with a goal of acquiring ten years of data. One more caveat: this is new habitat, not restoration. It was sunk in an area that was mostly sand, so no existing reef habitat was disturbed or restored. This is a net-new ecosystem for the region. The iconic ship’s two sixty-five-foot funnels, propeller, and radar mast are headed to a land-based museum near Destin. Everything else now belongs to the Gulf. Like the other divers who attended the sinking, I was hoping to dive it within the first 24 hours. But the rough conditions forecast for today, which pushed the sinking up one day, also kept us out of the water. I’ll be back as soon as I can to skim above the deck, but the bragging rights for the vessel’s first recreational dive are still up for grabs. The exact date divers will have access to the new dive site is still unknown. Safety divers must clear the site before recreational divers are allowed. Local charter operators are hoping to head out as soon as Friday. Niuhi Dive Charters says divers from all over the world have already signed up. The county says her top deck, anticipated to be at 55 to 60 feet, is accessible to all levels of certified divers, which makes an Open Water certification the entry ticket. If you want more than a look at the top, Advanced Open Water, with its 100-foot-limit, is the better choice, and charter operators set their own requirements. Wreck and Nitrox certifications are smart additions. The lower decks belong to technical divers with decompression and trimix training. Plan on a full day offshore. She’s about twenty-two nautical miles southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach, and Destin is the closest launch point. Divers can book through Niuhi Dive Charters or ScubaTech Destin, which runs daily Gulf charters aboard the Sea Cobra. Alexandra Gillespie is the former digital editor of Scuba Diving magazine. With nearly 200 dives under her weight belt, and has covered scuba diving and marine sustainability for Outside, National Geographic, U.S. News and World, NPR, BBC, and other major publications. She’s gone diving everywhere from California’s kelp forests to Bahamian reefs to Sudan’s Red Sea.

item.title: JSX brings semi-private flights to Boston with 2 new routes
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
JSX is bringing its popular semi-private flights to Beantown. The boutique air carrier plans to begin flying from Boston this winter, JSX said this week. The company's service will be based out of the nearby Laurence G. Hanscom Field (BED) in the town of Bedford, Massachusetts. The Boston service will launch with a route to New York City on Feb. 8, followed by flights to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport (OPF) in Florida beginning on Feb. 11. JSX will operate four daily flights between Boston and New York from Monday through Friday, with two flights on Saturday and three on Sunday. The Miami service will run once per day five times a week: Monday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Notably, JSX did not specify which New York airport would host the Boston flights. A spokesperson did not immediately answer TPG’s request for further details. JSX typically flies to New York’s Teterboro Airport (TEB) and Westchester County Airport (HPN), although various restrictions set by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey mean that JSX cannot publicly promote TEB as a destination. Because of those restrictions, anyone looking to fly to or from New York has to sign up for the free Club JSX program, which offers rewards and has no minimum spending or flying requirements. Passengers can also earn United MileagePlus miles under a partnership between the two companies. The carrier will use its Embraer E145 aircraft on both routes, which can seat up to 30 passengers in a 1-1 configuration. Fares start at $199 one-way between Boston and New York, with one-way flights between Boston and Miami starting at $599. “Greater Boston represents an exciting new chapter for JSX, marking our first entry into Massachusetts and an important milestone in the continued expansion of our East Coast network,” JSX CEO Alex Wilcox said in a statement. “As one of the nation's leading centers for business, innovation, and higher education, Greater Boston is a natural fit for our unique approach to flying,” he added. How JSX makes private-jet convenience available to the public JSX operates as a “hop-on charter” service, which essentially operates private charter flights that anyone can buy a seat on. It means that JSX flights operate more like private flights than commercial, using posh private Fixed-Base Operators (FBOs) instead of public airport terminals and allowing passengers to venture from curb to seat in just 20 minutes. The flight experience itself is equally luxurious with no middle seats, lots of legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, complimentary snacks and drinks and checked luggage that’s returned right at the side of the plane. Overall, the service pitches the idea of private jet convenience for a fraction of the cost. The public charter service — which does not bill itself as an “airline,” due to different regulations between charter carriers and public airlines — operates out of 29 airports across the U.S. and Mexico. Although private jet passengers typically bypass TSA screening, JSX implemented a more thorough in-house screening process in 2025 to address security concerns. Still, the process is remarkably quicker than going through the public terminal, making JSX an appealing option for those looking to skip the hassle of a regular flight. JSX's flights from Boston are already on sale, with service scheduled to start in February. With the entry to New England, JSX adds its 29th city, and brings its own entry to the competitive business of moving premium travelers between Boston and New York. Related reading:

item.title: REVIEW: The new London restaurants to try in November 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
We've always got one eye on any new restaurants opening on the London food scene. Our editors are on the ball for the latest openings in each London neighbourhood, from Covent Garden restaurants to Shoreditch hotspots. For the ultimate list of places to eat in the city, check out our definitive guide to London's best restaurants. These are the places that we consider the crème de la crème, from generations-old spots that have stood the test of time and Michelin-starred dining rooms that get better each year to mind-blowing new openings from this list that we decided deserved a spot on the ultimate round-up of the best restaurants in London. For new restaurants opening in London recently, we've seen follow-ups from some of the city's biggest-name chefs and a handful of restaurant openings that have stopped us in our tracks: from London's newfound love for BBQ to a Turkish restaurant that's turning heads. These are our favourite openings of the past six months. How we choose the tastiest new restaurant openings in London The best new restaurants in London are the most exciting places to eat that have just opened in the capital city. Ranging from small affairs with daily changing menus from up-and-coming chefs to Michelin-starred spots with fresh new menus, these are London's new restaurants we've got our eye on right now. Every restaurant on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has eaten at that restaurant. When choosing new restaurants, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for stand-out dishes, a great location, warm service, and serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new restaurants open in London. Best new London restaurants in November 2026 Following the devastating fire that destroyed beloved Endo at the Rotunda in September 2025, a hole has been left in London’s dining scene ever since. So, when news of Endo Chelsea broke, it may come as no surprise that securing one of the 10 seats in the intimate omakase felt akin to getting your hands on Glastonbury tickets. The new West London outpost is darker and sexier yet distinctly more traditional than its predecessor at the Rotunda. Inspired by the sushi counters of the 1920s and 30s, the atmosphere is theatrical and practically electric as we wait for the star of the show to appear. I take my seat, sip my delicious tea-infused Negroni, and watch as the seamlessly choreographed 19-course performance unfolds. Undoubtedly, Endo is the star of this show, handing each guest a piece of sushi and swapping tales at the same time. From the beautifully ornate sake cups, designed and handcrafted by Endo himself, to the three varieties of rice used throughout the omakase, each paying homage to one of his great teachers. The food is, unsurprisingly, exceptional. Local produce meets Japanese technique. Much of tonight’s fish comes from Cornwall, where Endo recently lived and worked alongside local fishermen. Highlights include langoustine nigiri, turbot and mackerel, alongside an oyster paired with a cup of exceptional 200-year-old discontinued sake. Then there’s the Wagyu with cep mushroom and chive. Three hours slip past in the blink of an eye. A triumphant new chapter, this new opening is like a phoenix rising from the ashes. Welcome to the new church of Endo. Lucy Bruton Address: 8-9 Blacklands Terrace, London SW3 2SP This isn’t just a new restaurant to try in London, Lunette is the new restaurant in London. The debut solo restaurant of chef Florence Knight, previously of Sessions Art Club and Polpetto, has all the hallmarks of an A-list haunt. There’s the swishy address – squirrelled down a 10th-floor corridor and up some glossy stairs within St. Clement, the first hotel from Soho House founder Nick Jones since he stepped back from the private members’ club. There’s design-showroom good looks in the long dining room with purposefully incongruous tables: steel rectangles, glossy round tables and a cream sofa seating area in the middle for the truly brave. And then of course, the million-pound Thames views with an outdoor terrace that is destined to have its own waitlist come summer. Rare for these seen-and-be-seen spots, though, the food is actually great. So phenomenal, in fact, I found myself scraping every last morsel and sliver of sauce from each plate. The four-course lunch and six-course supper menu is plainly worded but is anything but. Runner bean, squid and yarrow translates to a bright green bowl of fresh herby magic. Equally dazzling is the marigold orange of the cock crab, pepper and yolk, a lick-the-plate-clean egg-jammy, buttery risotto with a footnote of peppery heat. I was sceptical of the custard, onion and caviar, with the latter ingredient often used so haphazardly that it lost all appeal. This is where Knight’s restraint really shines – the caviar is respectfully the star rather than a hedonistic afterthought. There’s a masterful light and shade with each dish, along with the option for wine pairings to really hit the high notes. If you go it alone, most bottles of wine are under £100, which is refreshing. Likewise, the £16 signature martini is poured in two servings into the daintiest glasses. With two pudding courses, I left full, happy and wondering how long it will take until a Michelin star comes calling. Lauren Burvill Address: 180, The Thames, 12 Temple Place, Temple, London WC2R 2NF I must admit, I never thought a hole-in-the-wall this charming could exist a few steps from London’s chaotic Strand. But on a gloomy work night, when I walked into this new bistro housed in an old church furniture workshop, it felt like the place had been here for decades. The comfort food here is straight out of a French farmhouse, with a subtle British touch. It’s all bursting with flavour, with portions large enough to satisfy you, while leaving room for the next course. We start off our evening with a one-bite raw beef croustade dusted with comté and, because I can never get enough of my favourite French cheese, moved on to a tarragon-topped comté quiche that I know will become a post-work staple. The mains are French classics that weave in local fare (think stuffed cabbage chou farci but with pigeon); we opt for delectable grilled mackerel in a rich lobster bisque, and what might officially be one of my top three comfort dishes in London: the hen of the woods (a sponge-sized nutty mushroom that grows around oak trees) and armagnac vol-au-vent with sauce Parisienne. I grew up with my mother making vol-au-vent, so enjoying a forest-y twist on such a nostalgic dish was a treat. For dessert we shared an unbeatable chocolate mousse drizzled with olive oil and sprinkled with flaky salt, and one of my favourite French desserts: black fig clafoutis. For those unfamiliar, this eggy, crustless tart typically uses whole cherries, so not having to worry about the pits with this version was a win-win. Tamara Southward Address: 42 Maiden Lane, Covent Garden, WC2E 7LJ It’s not often I find myself dining at the same restaurant twice in one week, but The Horses is such a hot ticket right now that it’s no surprise when one of my more switched-on foodie friends excitedly tells me that she’s booked us lunch there a few days after my first visit. And I have no problem returning – this latest outpost from Public House Group (The Hart in Marylebone, The Pelican in Notting Hill) hits all their signatures: top-drawer UK produce, served simply and beautifully, in an elevated homage to the great British pub. The Horses dates back to 1790, and has been revamped by PHC with a traditional pub on the ground floor and three levels of seafood dining on top, a nod to the former Smithfield fish market nearby. Downstairs is heaving when we arrive on Friday night, but escaping up a back staircase we enter into the relative calm of the dinky oyster bar. There’s a subtle sea theme running through the design, with limewashed ceilings, soft curtains reminiscent of sails or netting, orb lights hung with chains, and an ice-packed treasure chest of crustaceans overseeing it all from the horseshoe-shaped counter bar. It’s candlelit, intimate and wonderfully romantic. The chatty staff have a genuine enthusiasm for seafood – we get tips on which order to eat the oysters, freshly shucked in front of us, and whether they need a drop of homemade chilli sauce or mignonette. The cod’s roe on smoked bread is basically fancy taramasalata on toast and a fantastic pub snack, but the standout starters are the clams and cockles in a creamy, cider-y broth and the moreish squid coated in fried pastry crumbs with chilli mayo. Among the mains, the fish is the thing – there are six to choose from, plus specials, and six sauces to mix and match (“they’re actually all free right now, so I’d just go mad,” murmurs our waitress). Monkfish with langoustine gravy is satisfyingly meaty, and John Dory with the surprising recommendation of peppercorn sauce really works; but the star is the Dover Sole with garlic butter, accompanied by a pile of new potatoes studded generously with garlic, and sea greens. It all feels special but not stiffly formal, and I’ll be back yet again for pub snacks and pints in the near future. Olivia Squire As a Notting Hill resident with the luck of a job that’s given me dibs on newly opened restaurants, being at the centre of the anticipation is always exciting. But the lead-up to Nakimushi opening its doors felt quieter, as if those who’d caught a glimpse wanted to keep the place a secret immediately. On the affordable end compared to its sister restaurant Eel, Nakimushi is the marriage of Urchin and Robin’s Ramen – two former London residencies that now see chefs Yuji Shimokawa and Robin Kosuge bring opposite ends of Japanese cuisine together. We share wild hamachi with nori oil, vegetable ohitashi worth it for the mushrooms alone, and a tuna summer roll with blackberry and hibiscus (my favourite). For our mains, we choose lobster ramen with sobrassada and pistachio matcha ramen with daikon cress. If the veggie broth at a restaurant is this decadent (not to mention, healing), it’s a winner in my opinion. The ground floor is communal-style, where you watch your food being prepped in an open kitchen from counter seating or a shared table. But weave up the Scandi-style stairwell and you’re in a proper dining room, whose timber walls are covered with cool contemporary art and bottles of Japanese whisky. There’s only one dessert on the menu, the mugi-cha creme caramel; the only area I’d like to see revisited. It’s good, but perhaps not enough to warrant single status. Tamara Southward Romy Gill has been a permanent fixture on the London food scene for more than a decade. Since the unfortunate 2019 closure of her first restaurant, Romy’s Kitchen, in South Gloucestershire, Romy has become a welcome sight on TV screens between the release of three cookbooks – the latest being Romy Gill's India: Recipes from Home, in 2024. Being such a household name, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that her new venture, Romy Gill at The Pem, is the chef’s first restaurant in six years. It’s the aforementioned cookbook that greets us as we pass over the threshold, after weaving through Conrad London St. James, into a fantastically crimson dining space. Privacy panels divide the restaurant's heart into booth hideouts that feel more intimate than the sprawling space they’re set in, while tables along each side offer corners where besotted foodies feast under subdued lamplight. Cocktails arrive, the taste of cumin curiously coating my palate as I sip on the Malhar, crafted with Amrut Single Malt and homemade cumin syrup – the Anarkali isn’t to my taste, but a Negroni obsessive’s dream, I’m sure. Starters land and the feast begins as we pluck decoratively presented king prawns (and king they are) from their heads and savour melt-in-the-mouth tandoori lamb chops. The highlight, however, is the samosa chaat; a crisp samosa topped with chickpeas, sev, pomegranate seeds and yoghurt in a sensational jumble of taste and texture that we long to do all over again. Heaps of rice and chunks of torn naan, fresh out of the charcoal tandoor, come into action, soaking up the sweet butter chicken sauce before our waiter performatively surrounds the hake moilee in a refreshing, vibrant curry leaf broth. After initial insistence that we need no dessert, we cave and coat sugar-dusted churros in a decadent chocolate sauce – a perfectly gluttonous finish, after all, to a warming meal that ushers us gently into the autumn months. Connor Sturges Address: Romy Gill at The Pem, 22-28 Broadway, London SW1H 0BH Best new London restaurants in September 2026 There’s something ever so cool about anonymity, and as I walked straight past the door of Kid in Soho, I had to remind myself of this. There are no signs, bells or whistles here, just a rusty brown door with an almost imperceptible goat symbol marked on it. Kid holds a quiet, understated vibe that oozes confidence – and rightly so. The hotly anticipated restaurant is the latest project from former Mangal II chef Sertaç Dirik, who’s teamed up with David Carter of London mainstays Oma, Agora and Smokestak, making it quite the force to be reckoned with. Inside, the vibe is dimly lit, with exposed brick and a bustling open kitchen, reaching far beyond what the subtle exterior might at first suggest. The menu, meanwhile, is Turkish-inspired but with plenty of twists, blending a lovely mix of soul-soothing, comforting classics with an elevated execution. Highlights included the balloon-like tombik pide (worth visiting for alone), a smoked aubergine dip topped with whisker-thin grains, and the İçli Köfte – the most sumptuous ball of dry-aged beef, juicy and flavoursome, that will be living in my mind rent-free for a while. Of course, most customers opt for the namesake shoulder of goat on the menu, served in a huge traditional clay pot and slow-cooked overnight for the ultimate fall-away meat. Interestingly, the wine list is ordered not just by region, but by when wine-making practices first began in each destination. We opted for a light Cypriot glass to match the restaurant's tone and offset some of the richer dishes. So, is the new kid on the block actually worth the hype? I’d say yes – and I’d even hazard a guess that this new dining address has some seriously long-standing appeal. Lucy Bruton Address: Kid, 53-55 Frith Street, London W1D 4SJ One could be forgiven for thinking this rather enviable London postcode – on W1S’s Cork Street – can be a little pretentious at times. But that’s certainly not the case at Bar Finch. Perusing the menu prior to arrival, I felt – dare I say – a touch underwhelmed. Burgers and chips, Caesar salad, roast chicken; you know the drill. But that’s not the case either. What you actually get when you patter down the steps is a new, polished neighbourhood go-to that feels akin to plopping yourself down in a very chic living room, complete with terribly friendly staff and the cheerful spirit of a proper Italian bacaro. Ashy wood panelling and lashings of texture keep things cosy, while great slabs of marble wherever you look remind you that you’re still firmly in Mayfair. Suitably settled in our plush leather booth, we got stuck in. The menu, a triumph of Italian-tinged comfort food, now makes sense. Portion sizes are perfect for sharing (and actually so – not just billed that way on the menu only to arrive disappointingly tiny). The hand-rolled pastas were most popular among fellow diners, arriving tossed in silky, slow-cooked ragù, while a tomato salad and a side of beans tasted as fresh as anything you’ll eat all week. The steak has a delightfully indulgent thread of marbling that rivals the tabletops, and proper crispy chips, but the dish to order is the chicken piccata – complete with a salty, crackling skin curled up pleasingly at the edges and a generous smattering of oily capers for good measure. Drinks pairings are treated with equal flair. There’s a curated wine list featuring both indie Italian winemakers and classic European vintages, but you won’t feel shortchanged if you skip them all and go straight for the cocktails, which are far too good to miss. All the Italian classics are present, but the standout – promptly earning a second order – was the Champs-Élysées; bright with lemon and Green Chartreuse, given a grown-up edge with a hit of cognac. Whatever you do, don’t leave without ordering the tiramisu, which is utterly huge (so don’t say you weren’t warned). Make sure to leave room, as taking leftovers home isn’t allowed. But who cares, in any case? This is a delightful spot to hunker down on a cold and gloomy evening at leisure. There’s no need to rush away so soon. Charley Ward At the start of September, husband-and-wife team Gabriel Waterhouse and Patricia Wakaimba opened the doors to Waterhouse, a much-anticipated restaurant, wine bar and garden set inside a Victorian warehouse on buzzing cobbled Ezra Street, just off Columbia Road Flower Market.
