Relatively unknown, with only a single scuba diving lodge that has direct access to it, this place is the third-largest coral reef system in the world. More than three-quarters of all coral species known to science live and grow here, as do more than half of all recognized fish. The Great Sea Reef, nicknamed the GSR, is also a growing hub of conservation research. In July 2026, a new partnership between the Professional Association of Diving Instructors (PADI), PADI AWARE (the affiliated NGO), and the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) was launched to push community-backed ocean conservation. A key part of this is PADI AWARE’s new Global Shark & Ray Census, an ambitious project to collect data that PADI and WWF can use to inform governments, in Fiji and beyond, for the creation of new Marine Protected Areas. This recent collaboration made our morning shark sighting even more exciting—and meaningful. “We are bringing together PADI’s 30-million-plus certified divers and 6,600 dive centers with WWF’s conservation work in over 100 countries,” says Ian Campbell, a driving force behind the collaboration and the programs director of PADI AWARE. In visiting the GSR, I was experiencing firsthand how travelers can experience this ecosystem and be a part of an innovative approach to protecting coral reefs. When I saw the lone bull shark, I wrote “bull shark: 1” in my waterproof notebook. The scribble was below my other excited notes from that same dive that read: “leopard shark! Amazing: 1” and “white-tipped reef shark: 2”. This underwater note-taking is the first step of the shark and ray census; the logging would happen when we returned to land. When our dive ended a few minutes later, I rose to the surface, joining a group of scuba divers who were scrambling aboard our aluminum boat. Everyone, including Leone Vokai, founder of Great Sea Reef Divers and the diver who’d signaled the shark, was grinning. We stripped out of our gear and soaked wetsuits, whooping and chattering, as Leone’s crew passed out mugs of warming lemongrass tea and ginger cookies. The boat angled toward the shoreline and picked up speed: it was time to get back to the resort for a seafood lunch and logging. Awaiting us, past a sandy beach and the angled heights of coconut trees, was Nukubati resort (pronounced Noo-koom-bah-ti). As the sole property located on the Great Sea Reef, Nukubati is the labor of love of two Fijian generations: It was opened in 1992 by Fiji-born Jenny Leewai and her Australian husband, Peter Bourke; and is now helmed by their daughter, Lara, with her husband, Leone, who was born and raised on the nearby Mali Island. Set against the slow pulse of the waves, styled in classic, custom-ordered cane palm furniture atop gleaming wooden floors, this little haven delivered a peaceful welcome after every dive. Following a hot shower in my private bure, or bungalow, I rejoined the others at the broad open-air lounge, nicknamed the pavilion, which serves as the heart of this intimate resort. Jenny was already there, barefoot in a caftan with Champagne-colored pearls at her ears and fingers. Lara was there too, a red hibiscus flower tucked behind her ear. Lara and Leone’s young son, Masei, pattered past on the shining wooden floor, followed by a russet, tail-wagging dog, Bēbē. In this deeply relaxed atmosphere, alfresco lunches can last hours. But as soon as we finished the meal—spicy pawpaw soup, followed by skewers of whitefish, pineapple, onions, and peppers in a bed of peanut sauce—I gathered with the other divers around a coffee table, where a weatherbeaten copy of Tropical Pacific Fish lay. There, PADI regional manager Robyn Vincent and Leone led us through a lecture on sharks and rays, which ranged in topics from biology (many sharks are late bloomers: the remarkable greenland shark, for example, doesn’t reach sexual maturity until it’s 100 years old) to shark tourism (each year, roughly 500,000 people dive specifically to see sharks around the world, creating an industry valued at $314 million USD). Then, we logged the sharks we’d just seen on the PADI AWARE app. Tapping through the details took just me six minutes as I marked our location (a dive site called “Fish Market”), our activity (options include diving, snorkeling, boating, fishing, and others), our maximum underwater depth (60 feet), and the number and species of sharks I’d seen (one bull shark, two gray reef sharks, one whitetip reef shark, and one zebra shark). Since the census launched in April 2026, more than 212,000 people have participated, submitting thousands of sightings from around the world. That data is vetted by employees at PADI AWARE, with scientific support from the James Cook University Centre for Sustainable Tropical Fisheries and Aquaculture in Australia. And what’s been logged so far is already being used: According to the university, some data has been implemented in a scientific paper currently under review, and verified images submitted to the app have helped confirm the presence of four shark and ray species in the neighboring country of Vanuatu. One of those four, the great hammerhead shark, is listed as ‘Critically Endangered’ on the IUCN Red List. These awe-inspiring animals can grow up to 20 feet long and engage in mysterious mating rituals, swimming in synchronous, ascending spirals. Their very existence off the reef-fringed, tropical shores of Vanuatu had been debated by scientists—until now. Thanks to PADI’s presence in remote natural places like these, the census’s fast-accumulating data could also have ramifications in PADI and WWF’s efforts to help reach the UN Convention on Biological Diversity’s 30x30, the goal to protect 30% of the world’s oceans by 2030. “WWF brings the political clout,” says Cheryl Bowlin, the founder of Reef Stewardship Frameworks, a community-based conservation nonprofit in Fiji. “They help encourage policy to create Marine Protected Areas.” Those Marine Protected Areas keep reefs healthy and safe for locals and travelers alike, and can provide new forms of income to communities. (An academic paper published in 2025 found that turning unprotected dive sites into fully protected marine areas could generate more than $2 billion globally in direct tourism revenue—an income stream that largely incorporates dive centers owned and run by locals.) Places like Nukubati Resort are a prime example of the reach and impact that travelers can have, even if they might not realize it at first. During my five-day stay there, I saw multiple species of sharks and rays—utterly wild, without human influence of feeding or baiting—on every single dive. Stats like that make scuba diehards and casual passersby alike take notice, especially since diving on the GSR is an option for all skill levels, from snorkelers to beginner divers (like me) to advanced. Visitors can experience top-notch diving and contribute helpful data at the same time. “I’ve been working as a PADI scuba diving instructor since 2013, and I’ve traveled and dived extensively all over the world,” Vincent said as we motored out to a dive site the following day, where a gentle current carried us over seawalls coated with hard corals and neon fish. “The fact that we’ve seen sharks on every single dive, and we are the only boat here, is incredible. There could be 50 dive centers here, 50 other dive boats.” The reef holds significance in local heritage, too. “The name of the Great Sea Reef in our northern dialect is Bainivualiku, which means the fence of the north,” said Leone. We sat at Nukubati, along with Leone’s wife and business partner, Lara, not far from the beach one afternoon, after another morning of glorious diving. “In the old days, the reef protected our community from sailing invaders who wanted to come in,” he said. The Great Sea Reef has been celebrated in songs and stories amongst regional communities for generations. Today, Leone and other locals are recognized as traditional stakeholders in the GSR’s future. To them, “The reef is our heart and soul,” Leone said. That unshakable faith is evident in the family’s nurturing of Nukubati, which has withstood cyclones, a fire, the COVID-19 pandemic, and more. Throughout the trials the property has come out the other side, a timeless hideaway that accommodates a maximum of just 14 guests. The strong family and community bonds have kept it going; 100 percent of the Nukubati staff are local. Sustainability is another defining aspect, as Nukubati has run on solar panels, a system hand-engineered by co-founder Peter, since its opening day in the 1990s. Fast forward to now: In September 2026, Nukubati and its in-house operator, Great Sea Reef Divers, were recognized as a PADI Eco Center, a designation awarded to properties that demonstrate a significant commitment and investment to conservation and sustainability. Now, after their dives, Leone and his team log the sharks and rays they’ve seen in the new global census, and encourage visitors to join. “There's no looking back now,” Leone said, rubbing his hands together. Ahead of him, the Great Sea Reef—colossal, colorful, teeming with sea life and yet empty of humans—waited just below the surface.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Hike of the Week: Explore a Wilderness With Wolves and Endless Flat-Topped Peaks
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
The Flat Tops Wilderness Area in northwestern Colorado is one of my favorite places to drop off-grid. Among its basalt peaks and sweeping valleys are some of the state’s best trails, in my opinion. Its “hidden-gem” days are long gone—lots of people, especially those from Colorado’s Western Slope, recreate here. Yet, you can still find areas where you’re the only human for miles. That solitude can be intoxicating. The 10.9-mile out-and-back to Marvine Lakes via the Marvine Trail could easily be a dayhike. But when I visited with a group of friends this summer, we wanted to spend time marinating in the scenery, lounging on the lakes’ shoreline with some beers, and enjoying a nice bagged meal with friends. I saw more wildlife on that trip than I have on any other in a long time: We crossed paths with elk, mule deer, beavers, and a silver-colored canid that looked much bigger than any coyote I’ve ever seen. Was it a wolf? I can’t say with certainty, but the Flat Tops is one of the areas where Colorado’s wolf reintroduction program has been most successful. The trail starts at East Marvine Campground, about 35 miles east of Meeker. When we arrived, several outfitters were saddling horses and preparing to ride out with their groups. The trail is multi-use, though mountain bikes and motorized vehicles are not permitted in wilderness areas. Dogs are allowed, and leashes are not required. But hikers should stay both stay horse- and bear-aware. The hike itself isn’t too strenuous, climbing just 1,045 feet over the 5.4 miles to the lakes. It passes small beaver ponds, pops out into meadows where you might catch a glimpse of browsing elk or deer, and winds through thick old-growth pine and spruce forest. The hike follows pristine Marvine Creek the entire way. Water is never an issue as long as you’ve got a means of purifying it. When you arrive at lower Marvine Lake, you’ll find turquoise water reflecting the stratigraphy of the towering cliffs that hem the valley. The trail splits and goes around both sides of the lake, passing dispersed camping spots. We picked one on the very far end of lower Marvine Lake, between it and upper Marvine Lake. Our group hung out well past dark, expecting the kind of stars that only the remote corners of the Rockies can deliver. We were not disappointed. We hiked out the next day, retracing our footsteps to the trailhead. If you wanted a longer hike, the Marvine Trail extends deeper east into the Flat Tops Wilderness Area and connects to an entire trail network. Following it all the way out to Twin Lakes and returning via the East Marvine Lakes Trail would make a 22.5-mile loop and end at the same trailhead you started at, with more alpine ponds and lakes along the way.

item.title: America’s Most Famous Ocean Liner Is Sent to a Watery Grave—and a New Life
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
In a secluded corner of Mobile, Alabama, past train tracks, deserted lots, and a county jail, sits a treasure of American history: the SS United States. The country’s flagship ocean liner, once proudly painted red, white, and blue, is now faded and marred by rust. Today, rather than sailing the silver swell of Atlantic waves, it sits in the flotsam-filled murk of the Mobile River. Yet even in the ship’s diminished state, I was awestruck by the sheer force of her towering presence when I paid her a visit on a sticky August afternoon. I wondered: What life remained in the SS United States yet? At nearly 1,000 feet long, the SS United States has always occupied a world of superlatives. When she was built in the early 1950s, she was the largest ocean liner ever constructed entirely in the United States, measuring a cool 100 feet longer than the RMS Titanic and boasting five more decks than the doomed British passenger liner. To this day, SS United States still holds the record for the fastest transatlantic crossing by an ocean liner, made on her maiden voyage in July 1952 when she tore from New York City to the United Kingdom in just 3 days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes. She regularly hosted the biggest names of the time, from artistic celebrities like Marilyn Monroe, Salvador Dalí, and Marlon Brando, to former presidents and first ladies like Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower, and Eleanor Roosevelt. Those glory days did not last. In November 1969, the crew had just disembarked from the ship’s 400th voyage when they were abruptly informed that it had been their last. A perfect storm of affordable passenger jet travel, rising oil and labor costs, and the withdrawal of government subsidies had put the SS United States out of business after only 17 years of passenger travel. She has since spent nearly six decades bouncing from buyer to buyer, searching for a purpose. Now, the storied liner at last has a new home and calling: She’s becoming the world’s largest artificial reef. On November 12, the SS United States will be sunk off the coast of Destin, Florida, where she will shelter dozens of species of fish and other marine life, and become a major destination for recreational divers and fishers. I had come to her current home in Alabama for a behind-the-scenes tour of her labyrinthine corridors and expansive decks—one of the last ever above water. Alex Fogg, the natural resources chief for Destin-Fort Walton Beach tourism, and the mastermind behind the project, was my guide for the day. Despite the blanket-like heat, we both wore long pants, closed-toe shoes, and white safety helmets. “We are going to be on a ship that has holes that have been cut in the floor, and there’s things above your head,” Fogg warned me. “So just be aware of where you’re stepping.” With that, we walked up a narrow plank leading to a small, rusted steel door on the ship’s towering port side. The light inside was dim, and came only from the gaps where glass windows and portholes once stood. We marched up a narrow spiral staircase to a deck two floors above, where the first-class cabins once were. The doors and walls had long since been removed, but outlines of the floor plans still remained etched into the metal, as did shower and toilet drains, giving an idea of how the poshest passengers lived on board. We climbed the remnants of a grand staircase, and reached a long indoor promenade deck that was once lined with floor-to-ceiling windows, but is was now exposedopen to the elements. The tour continued past empty lounges where copious martinis were no doubt served, and I imagined the ghosts of jazz bands past playing on now-hollowed-out stages. We passed the captain’s dining room, where the most elite guests took their meals, but now spiders were the only diners. On the bow, I took a photo for scale with the ship’s anchor—the largest I’d ever seen, resembling an ancient vertebra from some prehistoric leviathan. The tour wrapped up with a visit to the engine room, a jumble of pipes, catwalks and rails that were like a steampunk rendition of Chutes and Ladders. It was surreal to imagine all of this, the entirety of the SS United States, soon underwater, given over to the crustaceans and fishes and sea turtles. Marine life will likely arrive within hours of the ship sinking, Fogg says, but it will probably take at least a year for the ecosystem to fully blossom. Unlike other parts of Florida, the aquamarine waters off Destin-Fort Walton Beach lack an abundance of reef and other habitat that encourage a greater diversity and population of marine species. But artificial reefs can provide a substitute for these natural features. Thanks in part to Fogg’s leadership, more than 600 artificial reefs, ranging from small blocks of concrete to entire sunken ships, have already been installed in Destin-Fort Walton Beach since 2017, greatly boosting diving and fishing opportunities. Fogg had been looking for an iconic vessel to become the crown jewel of this program when he received a message from a contractor about the SS United States needing a new home. After Googling the ship, he realized it more than fit the bill. “I was like, ‘Man, I really want that,’” he told me. Despite the suitability of the ship for his needs, he had little idea of how complicated it would be to turn his vision into a reality. At the time, the ship was in Philadelphia, owned and cared for by a nonprofit organization called the SS United States Conservancy. Some conservancy officers and board members had family ties or personal histories with their group’s namesake vessel, however, and sinking it was, according to Fogg, “not their number one choice.” Board member Warren Jones, for example, was a passenger in 1961 and 1962. “It was just so unforgettable, sailing past the Statue of Liberty and just thinking, ‘Wow, we are going out to sea!’” Jones told me. He was just eight years old at the time of his sailings, but he still vividly remembers his time on board, including running through the black-and-silver first-class ballroom with his sister, watching Disney movies in the theater, and almost getting blown overboard by the North Atlantic wind. Jones, like others at the conservancy, originally hoped to find a developer who would refurbish the ship. But after various deals fell through—including one to turn her into a recreational destination at Pier 76 in Manhattan—their choices began to narrow. Fogg and his colleagues’ solution was much better than the alternatives, Jones admitted: “She’s not being scrapped, and she’s not just deteriorating at some pier somewhere.” Still, he said, “bittersweet is the best way to describe my feelings.” Purchasing the ship from the conservancy was only the first step. Getting her out of Philadelphia was another major feat, requiring a detailed survey and much negotiation with the Coast Guard. After finally arriving in Mobile in March 2025, the ship began an extensive environmental remediation process. The asbestos walls that once made up the cabins had already been removed years before, but a specialized team still had to spend the better part of a year cleaning out around 120 fuel tanks, scraping off loose paint, carting away debris, ripping out the old ventilation system, and responsibly disposing of toxic materials. The ship’s dozen elevators were also removed, in part because they were covered in grease, but also to aid in sinking the ship efficiently, by opening up a path for the air to escape. “When you deploy a vessel, you want the air to get out very quickly and the water to get in very quickly,” Fogg said. “If not, it’ll weeble-wobble and could potentially end up on its side.” The sinking will be carried out not with explosives, as was the past norm, but by opening valves connected to huge, disconnected boiler pipes to allow water to flood in. A naval architect on the project calculated that the ship will be fully submerged within 45 minutes after these valves are opened. Fogg and a few others will dive the wreck that very day to survey how she settled and remove mounted IMAX cameras that will capture video of the sinking. By the next day, according to Fogg, eager recreational divers will arrive. Above the waterline, visitor center exhibits and a land-based museum will also soon keep the ship’s legacy alive, filled with artifacts and stories that the conservancy has carefully preserved. Jones said he takes comfort in the truth that, once again, the SS United States will be a source of wonder and delight for the public. Of his time on board, he said, “It was a real feeling of joy. People were just so happy to be there.”
